aspects.says: A pattern's binding is in scope only in its own guard and arm, and a colon case can't fall into a case that declares a binding.
basis: section:A case With a Type Pattern Tests, Casts and Binds, and the First Case That Matches Wins
aspects.reason: the compiler enforces both rules, so no wrong solution compiles for a test to catch

aspects.says: A pattern switch tries its cases from the top and runs the first whose pattern matches and whose guard is true; cases are not ranked by how specific they are.
basis: section:A case With a Type Pattern Tests, Casts and Binds, and the First Case That Matches Wins

aspects.says: A local variable a guard reads must be effectively final, and an exception thrown in a guard propagates unchanged.
basis: section:A Guard Runs Only After Its Pattern Matches, and Again for Every Case That Tries It
aspects.reason: the first is a compile-time rule with no wrong solution that compiles, and the second is a plain property of Java expressions the page notes in passing

aspects.says: A guard runs only after its pattern matches, and again for every case that tries it, so a call in two guards runs twice; a call made once in the arm doesn't.
basis: section:A Guard Runs Only After Its Pattern Matches, and Again for Every Case That Tries It

aspects.says: A guarded case covers nothing for exhaustiveness, even when the guards together accept every value.
basis: section:Over a Sealed Type, Naming Every Permitted Subtype Is Exhaustive, and Only Unguarded Cases Count

aspects.says: The compiler doesn't evaluate guards, so overlapping guarded cases compile silently and their order decides which one wins.
basis: section:The Compiler Rejects a Case That an Earlier Case Always Wins, but It Does Not Read Guards

aspects.says: A switch with no default, compiled before a permitted subtype was added, throws MatchException when it meets that subtype; a default answers it instead.
basis: section:A Subtype Added After Compilation Reaches the Switch as MatchException

aspects.says: case null, default sends null and every unhandled type to one arm, so it fits only where missing and unsupported mean the same thing.
basis: section:null Matches Only case null; Neither default Nor case Object Does

aspects.says: A null selector matches only case null; without it the switch throws NullPointerException before any case, even with a default or a case Object o.
basis: section:null Matches Only case null; Neither default Nor case Object Does

aspects.says: Over a sealed type, an unguarded case for each permitted subtype makes the switch exhaustive with no default, so a new subtype stops the build at the switch, while a default absorbs it silently.
basis: section:Over a Sealed Type, Naming Every Permitted Subtype Is Exhaustive, and Only Unguarded Cases Count

aspects.says: A switch statement that uses a pattern or case null must be exhaustive, like a switch expression.
basis: section:A Switch Statement With Patterns Must Be Exhaustive Too

aspects.says: An unguarded case dominates every later case of its own type or a subtype, guarded or not, and javac refuses the later case; a default before a pattern case and a constant after its type are refused too.
basis: section:The Compiler Rejects a Case That an Earlier Case Always Wins, but It Does Not Read Guards
